title: Research Bite #50: The Five-Year Itch: Motivational Factors That Influence the Career Decisions of Early Career Teachers in England
author: Craig Barton
summary: Craig Barton's Research Bite #50 summarizes a qualitative study by Thomas Procter-Legg, Rebecca J. S. Snell, and Robert M. Klassen, published in the British Educational Research Journal (2025, Vol. 51, Issue 4, pp. 1623-1647), examining what drives early-career teachers (ECTs) in England to stay in or leave the profession. Working from interviews with 20 ECTs across state-funded primary, secondary, and special schools, the researchers used Self-Determination Theory as a lens, distinguishing 'push' factors that increase quitting intentions from 'pull' factors that reduce them. The central finding is that the increasing complexity and administrative burden of the role -- including managing students with Education, Health and Care Plans -- pushes ECTs toward anxiety and low self-efficacy, while a growing sense of belonging and professional identity pulls them toward staying. Crucially, autonomous motivation (acting from genuine volition rather than external pressure) emerged as the strongest protective factor against attrition in the first five years, the period with the highest rate of teacher turnover. The paper's contribution is applying SDT specifically to ECTs, a group previously underexplored through this theoretical lens.
points: The study's central claim -- that ECT retention hinges less on workload volume and more on whether teachers experience autonomy, competence, and relatedness -- reframes retention as a motivational design problem, not just a staffing problem.

Administrative burden tied to supporting students with EHCPs was identified as a specific driver of anxiety and low self-efficacy among ECTs, pointing schools toward targeted SEND-support workload relief as a retention lever.
Because the sample was only 20 ECTs across England, the findings are best read as a rich qualitative account of mechanism (why ECTs leave) rather than a generalizable predictor of attrition rates.

Fostering positive professional identity and genuine relational belonging in a school's first five years appears to do more for retention than one-off wellbeing initiatives, per the study's own emphasis.
The push/pull framing gives school leaders a diagnostic vocabulary: naming whether a specific ECT concern is a 'push' (drives them out) or a 'pull' (keeps them in) clarifies which lever to pull.
quotes: This academic article explores the motivational factors influencing early career teachers' (ECTs) decisions to stay or leave the profession in England. The study identifies key push and pull factors, such as the increasing complexity and relentlessness of the role, its emotional impact, alongside the profound sense of belonging and the development of a positive professional identity.

Teachers should remember that fostering a positive professional identity and cultivating meaningful relationships within the school community and with students are crucial. This autonomous motivation significantly reduces intentions to quit, supporting well-being and retention, especially in the first five years of their careers.

The study included 20 Early Career Teachers (ECTs) from state-funded primary, secondary, and special schools in England. All participants had less than 5 years' teaching experience. The group was diverse in age and gender, largely reflecting the demographics of teachers in England.

This paper uniquely applies Self-Determination Theory to explore the motivational needs and perspectives of Early Career Teachers (ECTs), an area previously underexplored. It identifies specific push and pull factors influencing their career decisions, highlighting that autonomous motivation reduces quitting intentions.

The increasing complexity of the teaching role impacts classroom practice by creating additional non-student-facing administrative duties. This can hinder teachers' ability to focus on student interaction and their core teaching responsibilities.

For example, managing the increasing number of students with Education, Health and Care Plans (EHCPs) adds to the administrative burden, potentially taking time away from direct teaching and support within the classroom. Teachers may feel ill-equipped to handle the multifaceted needs of students, leading to anxiety and low self-efficacy in the classroom.
